Notes From the HubSpot Refounding, Day 7 (Wed, Nov 18):

Writing this live from the HubSpot HQ. @bhalligan and I are having an all-day strategy meeting with the leadership team.

The one thing I need to get out there. We tried a new thing last week (on Day 1) of the refounding that just didn't work.

We tried out positioning HubSpot as the "Customer Relationship Harness".  

Rolled it out on the HubSpot home page (which gets a lot of traffic).

That positioning really didn't work. At all. A vast majority of people were either confused, irritated or both. Some were downright angry. A vanishingly small number of people liked it or loved it. 

This is one of the benefits of building in public (be it a product or company).  You get very rich feedback from the broader community. I got hundreds of comments on that harness positioning (if you were one of those commenters, thank you!)

So effective this morning, we're retracting that positioning. The HubSpot home page has been reverted.

Was this the best way to test broad, company positioning? Probably not. Was it effective and a net positive? Absolutely. 

The worst thing is not for people to dislike something you put out there. The worst thing is that people don't care at all and ignore it completely. This positioning faux pas let us know that there are a lot of people who care.

Thanks for your patience as we continue to work on the #HubSpotRefounding.

I can't promise you that we're going to get everything right, but I will promise that we'll listen, learn and iterate.

Cheers.

Notes From the HubSpot Refounding, Day 10 (Sat, Nov 21):

It's Saturday night, about 2:30am in Boston. @bhalligan and I exchanged a dozen emails today and several of them are doozies. Just like old times!

Oh, before I forget, if you've been following along the #HubSpotRefounding journey, no, you didn't miss some installments. I had started this process by posting daily, but then the schedule got really, really busy (had all day strategy meetings with the exec team followed by dinner with...the exec team...and night catching up on the day). Then doing that again the next day.

So, from here on in, I'm going to write once every whenever (which is much more my pace anyways).

Some notes from this week:

1) As much of an introvert as I am and as much as I believe in the pajama principle (iykyk), there's really nothing like being together with colleagues and strategizing, brainstorming and laughing. There's a lot of laughing...we're a collegial bunch. Intense, but collegial).

2) Brian and I have different business love languages. He loves a whiteboard (no whiteboard is going to stay blank for long if Brian comes within a few feet of it). I, on the other hand, am a words person. He thinks in visuals, I think in words. Not that I don't enjoy a good diagram (especially of the Venn variety) or that Brian can't put words together into sentences (he's quite good at it), we just both have our default modes.

3) One of the hardest things in a startup is coming up with the story -- the narrative. What *is* the company? What does it do? Why does it do that? What's the shift that caused the company to be created? It's one of the things we're working on right now. In a way, writing this narrative as part of a refounding is even harder than it was for the founding. Because HubSpot has been around for 20 years. There's already a couple of chapters of HubSpot that have been written. What we want to do as we write the next chapter is to honor our history but not let it block what we're trying to build next. Stay tuned...  

Now, it's time to get some sleep.  But first, a few more emails. :)

outsiders.name: Danny Postma
outsiders.text:
Here's my thought on the future of software/SaaS.

I'm completely switching off hosted platforms and hosted tools. I just reverse engineer them for myself, because I only need parts of them.

Two reasons why:

1. I want to own my data.

I use my data in different tools. Marketing, note-taking, whatever. And I want my agents, like Claude, to have complete access to it.

Not walled off in HubSpot, where I have to talk to their agent. Not behind MCP either. With MCP the agent pulls what it asks for, but it doesn't know what's there.

Give it a full list of data files and it has complete access. It knows what's there.

2. I want to customize it.

When I sign up for Pipedrive, I don't need all that bloated shit. I need one part of it, adjusted to my content, my business, how I work.

With AI that's a prompt, and one hour later it's done.

So static software is going to be a thing of the past. People want to adjust it to how they work and plug it into the other tools they have.

Where this goes, I think two ways:

A. You buy software again. Like paying $900 for a Photoshop license and putting it on your computer. Except now you get the source code. It's premade, because you don't have weeks to build it, but you host it on your own headless box and you can customize it, remove stuff, plug stuff in. Someone needs to build the operating system for this.

B. Everyone gets their own hosted instance. Not 10,000 customers on one box. Your own sandbox, with an agent that customizes it fully to you. The code stays proprietary, but you can adjust everything.

Might be completely wrong. Might be different for most people.

But this is already how I work.

virals.angle: Run a personal eval before you switch
virals.draft_en:
Everyone's arguing about Gemini 4 Neon vs Opus. Guillermo Rauch had an agent review his own coding sessions and pick the winner.

Do the same: replay your last 20 real tasks on both. Your codebase is the only benchmark that matters.

Both can't be true for your work. Post tokens/sec, RAM and one real task, then decide.

virals.angle: The AI-proof business is a room
virals.draft_en:
Greg Isenberg's top opportunity right now, 1.4M views and 32k bookmarks: build for loneliness.

The more AI fills feeds, the more people pay for real rooms, small groups and places with no cameras. Offline is turning into the premium product.

virals.draft_en:
Pieter Levels says AI reply spam on his posts is basically gone. His loop:
1. Anyone can report a bot
2. AI screens it
3. He checks their other replies
4. Block by user ID, so renames don't escape

Cheap AI first pass, human makes the call.

virals_narrative: Window Thu Nov 19 ~11:15 CT through Mon Nov 23 ~11:15 CT (catch-up after the Nov 20 run failed). Gemini 4 Neon owned the weekend: Theo's posts on it reached 1.0M and 573k, Logan's 'what are you building' prompt hit 487k, and Aravind reported fast usage growth on Perplexity, with a few loud counter-tests. The top watchlist post was Greg Isenberg's 'biggest opportunities' list (1.4M, 32k bookmarks), led by building for loneliness and camera-free places. Alex Finn pushed Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 as laptop-grade coding (256k and 224k, 5.5k bookmarks combined) while Theo argued open weights have never been further behind. Pieter Levels spent the window building out his AI-reply block list, and Danny Postma's 'rebuild only the SaaS parts you use' post (410k) was the most bookmarked builder idea. Outside the list: Elon's reach led as usual (Riemann proof, FSD V15, Grok Bot promos), Sam Altman flagged OpenAI's pretraining transparency post (1.7M), and Vercel launched audited zero-data-retention on AI Gateway. The meta: test models on your own work, demand receipts for local-model claims, and build things AI can't fake — rooms, trust, and owned data.

drafts.video_tip: 10s: a bloated CRM screenshot fading to a 3-feature page you built.

drafts.angle: Run a personal eval before you switch
drafts.draft_en:
Everyone's arguing about Gemini 4 Neon vs Opus. Guillermo Rauch had an agent review his own coding sessions and pick the winner.

Do the same: replay your last 20 real tasks on both. Your codebase is the only benchmark that matters.
drafts.inspired_by: @rauchg personal eval (45k) + @theo Neon (1.0M) + @OfficialLoganK (487k) + @AravSrinivas usage growth (73k) + @KIRASTUDI0 counter-test (81k)
drafts.video_tip: 9s: two terminals, same task list, tally of passes at the end.

drafts.draft_en:
Laptop models are the hype this weekend: Inkling 2 Small at 26B, Mini running in half a MacBook's memory. Theo says open weights have never been further behind.

Both can't be true for your work. Post tokens/sec, RAM and one real task, then decide.
drafts.video_tip: 8s: activity monitor + model output + a checklist of the three numbers.

drafts.angle: The AI-proof business is a room
drafts.draft_en:
Greg Isenberg's top opportunity right now, 1.4M views and 32k bookmarks: build for loneliness.

The more AI fills feeds, the more people pay for real rooms, small groups and places with no cameras. Offline is turning into the premium product.
drafts.video_tip: 10s: phones in a basket at the door, people talking at a table.

drafts.draft_en:
Pieter Levels says AI reply spam on his posts is basically gone. His loop:
1. Anyone can report a bot
2. AI screens it
3. He checks their other replies
4. Block by user ID, so renames don't escape

Cheap AI first pass, human makes the call.
drafts.video_tip: 9s: four-step flow animating left to right, ending on 'blocked'.
